{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"Ownership is a blunt word. If you buy a device, pay the full price, carry it home, and bear the cost when it breaks, then it should be yours. If its maker can reach back into it after the sale and switch off a feature you paid for, ownership isn't the relationship you have. You have a tenancy with unusually expensive furniture.

The maker will call this “software management,” “service adjustment,” or perhaps a necessary response to security and regulation. Some remote controls are useful; a patch that closes a dangerous vulnerability can protect you and everyone sharing the network. But usefulness doesn't settle authority. A locksmith may improve your lock (and you may welcome the visit), but that doesn't give the locksmith a permanent key or the right to brick your kitchen because your account changed.

Ask the practical question: after money changes hands, who gets the final say? If the answer is still the maker, then you didn't buy the whole device. You bought hardware wrapped around a revocable permission. The box may sit on your desk, the receipt may carry your name, and the repair bill may be entirely your problem – but the decisive switch remains somewhere else.

I start with that switch because it clears away a lot of contractual fog. I don't mean that every feature must work forever, or that a company must operate an online service without end. Servers cost money; components fail; laws change. A seller can state those limits before purchase and price the product accordingly. What it can't honestly do is advertise a capability, collect payment, and later redefine that capability as a favor it was merely lending you.

That arrangement is a shell game. Your money goes under the cup marked “sale”; the maker's continuing power hides under the cup marked “license” (the polite name for the trapdoor). When the cups stop moving, you've kept every burden associated with property while the seller has kept the most valuable privilege of ownership: deciding what the thing may do. That's bullshit with a user agreement attached.

The damage reaches beyond one annoyed customer. A worker can lose a tool needed for a job; a household can lose an accessibility feature; a small business can discover that equipment it budgeted for has changed underneath it (even if every physical component remains intact). Once we accept remote disablement as ordinary, we make every purchase contingent on the seller's future strategy – a strategy buyers neither control nor necessarily see.

I think the right policy test is narrower than a ban on updates and stronger than another disclosure box. If a post-sale change removes a material, advertised, paid-for function, the buyer should be able to refuse it, restore the function, receive a repairable local alternative, or obtain a meaningful refund. Security exceptions may be legitimate, but they shouldn't become a master key. The burden belongs on the party retaining remote power, because that party designed the dependency and can measure its risks.

We also need rules that protect the people who help owners resist disablement. If you can lawfully keep using a feature but can't obtain parts, install replacement software, or hire someone to restore it, your supposed remedy is a painted door on a brick wall. Repair and interoperability aren't side issues here; they're how we turn the abstract right to control a device into an available act.

I want us to use the honest vocabulary. A device subject to unilateral feature removal isn't fully sold. It is a bundle of permissions, some durable and some resting on the maker's patience. We can allow subscriptions, leases, and managed services when they are named and priced as such. But when a transaction is called a sale, our law should require the central fact of a sale: the seller lets go.","omitted":[],"refused":""}
